cards.label: Question 1 · 3 marks · Section A
cards.title: Question 1
cards.q: Suppose that \(f\) and \(g\) are in \(\mathcal{R}[a, b]\). If \(f(x) \le g(x)\) for all \(x \in [a, b]\), prove that \(\int_a^b f \le \int_a^b g\).

cards.label: Mark yourself 1 of 3 · up to 1 mark
cards.q: Did you set h = g - f and show h is nonnegative on [a, b]?

options.t: h = g - f defined and h(x) >= 0 shown from f(x) <= g(x)
h = g - f defined but nonnegativity not argued
No set-up, or the wrong sign for h

cards.why: Full marks need h = g - f with h(x) >= 0 justified from f(x) <= g(x) on [a, b].

cards.label: Mark yourself 2 of 3 · up to 1 mark
cards.q: Did you show h is integrable and every Riemann sum of h is nonnegative?

options.t: h integrable by linearity and each Riemann sum S(h;P) >= 0
Integrability of h stated but the sums not shown nonnegative
Neither point made

cards.why: Integrability of h follows from linearity; each Riemann sum S(h;P) of a nonnegative function is nonnegative.

cards.label: Mark yourself 3 of 3 · up to 1 mark
cards.q: Did you conclude integral g minus integral f is at least 0 by taking limits?

options.t: Limit of nonnegative sums gives integral h >= 0, so integral f <= integral g
Concludes the inequality without the limit step
No conclusion drawn

cards.why: Taking the limit of nonnegative sums gives the integral of h at least 0, so the integral of g is at least that of f.

cards.label: Model answer 1 of 3
cards.title: Set-up
cards.body: Let \(h = g - f\). Since \(f(x) \le g(x)\) for all \(x \in [a,b]\), we have \(h(x) \ge 0\) on \([a,b]\). Also \(h \in \mathcal{R}[a,b]\), by linearity of the integral.

cards.title: Picture
cards.body: f at most g: more area under g.
cards.label: Figure
Model answer 2 of 3
cards.title: Proof
cards.body: For any tagged partition \(P\) of \([a,b]\), the Riemann sum \(S(h;P)\) is a sum of nonnegative terms, so \(S(h;P) \ge 0\). Taking the limit as \(\|P\| \to 0\) gives \(\int_a^b h \ge 0\).

cards.label: Model answer 3 of 3
cards.title: Conclusion
cards.body: By linearity, \(\int_a^b h = \int_a^b g - \int_a^b f\). Hence \(\int_a^b g - \int_a^b f \ge 0\), that is \(\int_a^b f \le \int_a^b g\).

cards.label: Key line
cards.title: Key line
cards.body: h = g − f is non-negative and integrable, so its integral is non-negative.

cards.label: Key points
cards.title: Remember
points: Monotonicity: f <= g on [a,b] gives integral f <= integral g.
Put h = g - f; then h >= 0 and h is integrable by linearity.
Every Riemann sum of a nonnegative function is nonnegative.
A nonnegative limit gives integral h >= 0, so integral g - integral f >= 0.

cards.label: Question 3 · 3 marks · Section A
cards.title: Question 3
cards.q: State Cauchy’s Criterion and the Squeeze Theorem for the Riemann integrability of a function \(f : [a, b] \to \mathbb{R}\).

cards.label: Mark yourself 1 of 3 · up to 1 mark
cards.q: Did you state the Cauchy Criterion with eps, eta and tagged partitions P and Q?

options.t: Stated with eps, eta, tagged partitions P, Q and |S(f;P) - S(f;Q)| < eps
Stated in general form but the norm condition on P and Q is missing
Not stated, or wrong

cards.why: Full marks need: for every eps there is eta such that ||P||, ||Q|| < eta implies |S(f;P) - S(f;Q)| < eps.

cards.label: Mark yourself 2 of 3 · up to 1 mark
cards.q: Did you state the Squeeze Theorem with functions alpha, omega and integral(omega - alpha) < eps?

options.t: Stated with alpha <= f <= omega and integral(omega - alpha) < eps for every eps
Stated with the inequality but the integral condition is missing
Not stated, or wrong

cards.why: Full marks need alpha <= f <= omega, integrable, with the integral of omega minus alpha less than eps, for every eps.

cards.label: Mark yourself 3 of 3 · up to 1 mark
cards.q: Did you explain how each criterion is used to test integrability?

options.t: Cauchy compares Riemann sums; Squeeze traps f between integrable bounds
Gives one use only
No use stated

cards.why: Full marks need one use for each: Cauchy compares Riemann sums; Squeeze traps f between integrable bounds.

cards.label: Model answer 1 of 3
cards.title: Cauchy Criterion
cards.body: \(f \in \mathcal{R}[a,b]\) if and only if for every \(\varepsilon > 0\) there exists \(\eta_\varepsilon > 0\) such that \(|S(f;P) - S(f;Q)| < \varepsilon\) whenever \(P\) and \(Q\) are tagged partitions with \(\|P\|, \|Q\| < \eta_\varepsilon\).

cards.label: Model answer 2 of 3
cards.title: Squeeze Theorem
cards.body: \(f \in \mathcal{R}[a,b]\) if and only if for every \(\varepsilon > 0\) there are functions \(\alpha_\varepsilon, \omega_\varepsilon \in \mathcal{R}[a,b]\) with \(\alpha_\varepsilon \le f \le \omega_\varepsilon\) on \([a,b]\) and \(\int_a^b (\omega_\varepsilon - \alpha_\varepsilon) < \varepsilon\).

cards.label: Model answer 3 of 3
cards.title: Use
cards.body: The Cauchy Criterion tests integrability by comparing Riemann sums of f for fine tagged partitions. The Squeeze Theorem tests it by trapping f between integrable functions whose integrals differ by less than any \(\varepsilon\).

cards.label: Key points
cards.title: Remember
points: Cauchy: f in R iff Riemann sums of fine tagged partitions are close.
Squeeze: f in R iff for each eps there are alpha <= f <= omega with small gap.
Both are necessary and sufficient tests for Riemann integrability.
Cauchy uses the norm conditions ||P||, ||Q|| < eta; keep them in the statement.

cards.label: Question 5 · 3 marks · Section A
cards.title: Question 5
cards.q: Suppose that \(f : [a, b] \to \mathbb{R}\) is continuous on \([a, b]\), \(f(x) \ge 0\) for all \(x \in [a, b]\), and \(\int_a^b f = 0\). Prove that \(f(x) = 0\) for all \(x \in [a, b]\).

cards.label: Mark yourself 1 of 3 · up to 1 mark
cards.q: Did you assume, for contradiction, that f(c) > 0 at some point c in [a, b]?

options.t: Assumes f(c) > 0 for some c in [a,b] and sets up the contradiction
Assumption made but the contradiction is not stated
No assumption made

cards.why: Full marks need the contradiction assumption f(c) > 0 at some c, and the aim to show the integral is positive.

cards.label: Mark yourself 2 of 3 · up to 1 mark
cards.q: Did you use continuity to get an interval where f >= f(c)/2, and bound the integral below?

options.t: Interval from continuity with f >= f(c)/2, so integral f > 0
Interval from continuity given but no lower bound on the integral
No use of continuity

cards.why: Continuity gives an interval I of positive length around c where f >= f(c)/2; nonnegativity gives integral f > 0.

cards.label: Mark yourself 3 of 3 · up to 1 mark
cards.q: Did you conclude that the integral is positive, contradicting integral f = 0, so f = 0 everywhere?

options.t: Contradiction with integral f = 0 stated, hence f(x) = 0 on [a,b]
Contradiction found but the conclusion about f not stated
No contradiction

cards.why: The contradiction with integral f = 0 shows f(c) = 0 for every c, so f(x) = 0 on [a,b].

cards.label: Model answer 1 of 3
cards.title: Set-up
cards.body: Suppose, for contradiction, that \(f(c) > 0\) for some \(c \in [a,b]\). Since \(f \ge 0\), it is enough to show \(\int_a^b f > 0\), which contradicts \(\int_a^b f = 0\).

cards.label: Model answer 2 of 3
cards.title: Interval from continuity
cards.body: Let \(\varepsilon = f(c)/2 > 0\). By continuity there is \(\delta > 0\) with \(f \ge f(c)/2\) on the interval \(I = [c-\delta, c+\delta] \cap [a,b]\), which has positive length \(\ell(I)\). Since \(f \ge 0\), \(\int_a^b f \ge \int_I f\).

cards.title: Positive near c
cards.body: f ≥ f(c)/2 on an interval of positive length.
cards.label: Figure
Model answer 3 of 3
cards.title: Conclusion
cards.body: The lower bound is positive, so \(\int_a^b f > 0\). This contradicts \(\int_a^b f = 0\). Hence no such \(c\) exists, and \(f(x) = 0\) for all \(x \in [a,b]\).

cards.label: Key points
cards.title: Remember
points: Proof by contradiction: assume f(c) > 0 at some point c.
Continuity gives an interval around c where f >= f(c)/2.
Since f >= 0, the integral over [a,b] is at least that over I.
A positive lower bound contradicts integral f = 0, so f = 0 everywhere.

cards.label: Question 6 · 3 marks · Section A
cards.title: Question 6
cards.q: If \(f : [a, b] \to \mathbb{R}\) is continuous on \([a, b]\) with \(a < b\), prove that there exists \(c \in [a, b]\) such that \(\int_a^b f = f(c)(b - a)\).

cards.label: Mark yourself 1 of 3 · up to 1 mark
cards.q: Did you use the minimum m and maximum M of f to bound the integral by m(b-a) and M(b-a)?

options.t: Min m and max M attained; m(b-a) <= integral f <= M(b-a) by monotonicity
Min and max named but no integral inequality given
No bounds on the integral

cards.why: Full marks need min m and max M attained by continuity, and m(b-a) <= integral f <= M(b-a).

cards.label: Mark yourself 2 of 3 · up to 1 mark
cards.q: Did you define mu = (1/(b-a)) integral f and show m <= mu <= M?

options.t: mu = integral f / (b-a) shown to lie between m and M
Division done but betweenness of mu not argued
No mu defined

cards.why: Full marks need mu = integral f / (b-a) defined by dividing by b - a, and shown to lie between m and M.

cards.label: Mark yourself 3 of 3 · up to 1 mark
cards.q: Did you apply the Intermediate Value Theorem to get c with f(c) = mu, hence the result?

options.t: IVT gives c with f(c) = mu, so integral f = f(c)(b-a)
IVT mentioned but c or the final equation is missing
No IVT argument

cards.why: The Intermediate Value Theorem gives c with f(c) = mu, so integral f = f(c)(b-a).

cards.label: Model answer 1 of 3
cards.title: Bounds
cards.body: Since \(f\) is continuous on the closed interval \([a,b]\), it attains a minimum \(m\) and a maximum \(M\) there. Then \(m \le f(x) \le M\), so \(m(b-a) \le \int_a^b f \le M(b-a)\).

cards.label: Model answer 2 of 3
cards.title: Intermediate value
cards.body: Dividing by \(b - a > 0\), the number \(\mu = \frac{1}{b-a}\int_a^b f\) satisfies \(m \le \mu \le M\). By the Intermediate Value Theorem there is \(c \in [a,b]\) with \(f(c) = \mu\).

cards.body: The dashed rectangle has height f(c) and the same area.
cards.label: Figure
Key line
cards.title: Key line
cards.body: Intermediate Value Theorem.

cards.label: Model answer 3 of 3
cards.title: Conclusion
cards.body: Substituting \(f(c) = \mu\) gives \(\int_a^b f = f(c)(b-a)\). See the figure for the rectangle of height \(f(c)\) with the same area as the region under \(f\).

cards.label: Key points
cards.title: Remember
points: Continuous f on [a,b] attains a minimum m and a maximum M.
m(b-a) <= integral f <= M(b-a); divide by b - a.
mu = integral f / (b-a) lies between m and M.
The Intermediate Value Theorem gives c with f(c) = mu.

cards.label: Question 7 · 3 marks · Section A
cards.title: Question 7
cards.q: State the First Form of the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus. Explain why it cannot be applied to \(H(x) = 2\sqrt{x}\) and \(h(x) = H'(x) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{x}}\) on \([0, b]\).

cards.label: Mark yourself 1 of 3 · up to 1 mark
cards.q: Did you state the First Form of FTC with all its hypotheses and the conclusion?

options.t: All hypotheses stated and integral f = F(b) - F(a) given
Result stated but one hypothesis (continuity of F or finite set E) missing
Not stated, or wrong

cards.why: Full marks need f in R[a,b], F continuous on [a,b], F' = f except on a finite set E, and integral f = F(b) - F(a).

cards.label: Mark yourself 2 of 3 · up to 1 mark
cards.q: Did you check that H is continuous on [0,b] and H'(x) = 1/sqrt(x) on (0,b]?

options.t: H continuous on [0,b] and H'(x) = 1/sqrt(x) on (0,b]
H' found but continuity of H on [0,b] not checked
No check of H

cards.why: Full marks need H = 2 sqrt(x) continuous on [0,b] with H'(x) = h(x) = 1/sqrt(x) for x in (0,b].

cards.label: Mark yourself 3 of 3 · up to 1 mark
cards.q: Did you show h is unbounded near 0, so h is not in R[0,b] and the theorem does not apply?

options.t: h unbounded near 0, so h not in R[0,b]; hypothesis f in R[a,b] fails
Says h is unbounded but does not connect this to integrability
No reason given

cards.why: h = 1/sqrt(x) is unbounded near 0, so h is not in R[0,b]; the hypothesis f in R[a,b] fails.

cards.label: Model answer 1 of 3
cards.title: First Form
cards.body: Let \(f \in \mathcal{R}[a,b]\) and let \(E\) be a finite subset of \([a,b]\). If \(F\) is continuous on \([a,b]\) with \(F'(x) = f(x)\) for all \(x \in [a,b] \setminus E\), then \(\int_a^b f = F(b) - F(a)\).

cards.label: Model answer 2 of 3
cards.title: Check the derivative condition
cards.body: Take \(H(x) = 2\sqrt{x}\) and \(h(x) = 1/\sqrt{x}\) on \([0,b]\). \(H\) is continuous on \([0,b]\) and \(H'(x) = h(x)\) for \(0 < x \le b\), so the derivative condition holds with \(E = \{0\}\).

cards.label: Model answer 3 of 3
cards.title: Why it fails
cards.body: The function \(h\) is unbounded near \(0\), so \(h\) is not in \(\mathcal{R}[0,b]\). The hypothesis \(f \in \mathcal{R}[a,b]\) therefore fails, and the First Form cannot be used to evaluate \(\int_0^b h\).

cards.title: Graphs of H and h
cards.body: H = 2√x is continuous on [0, b]; h = 1/√x is unbounded near 0, so it is not integrable.

Key points
cards.title: Remember
points: First Form of FTC: f in R[a,b], F continuous, F' = f except on a finite set E.
Conclusion: integral of f over [a,b] equals F(b) - F(a).
The hypothesis f in R[a,b] is essential, not just F' = f.
h = 1/sqrt(x) is unbounded near 0, so h is not in R[0,b].

cards.label: Question 8 · 3 marks · Section A
cards.title: Question 8
cards.q: Using the First Form of the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus, show that there does not exist a continuously differentiable function \(f\) on \([0, 2]\) such that \(f(0) = -1\), \(f(2) = 4\), and \(f'(x) \le 2\) for \(0 \le x \le 2\).

cards.q: Did you note that f' is continuous, so f' is in R[0,2]?

options.t: f' continuous on [0,2], so f' in R[0,2] (continuous implies integrable)
Says f' is integrable but without the continuity reason
Not stated

cards.why: Full marks need f' continuous on [0,2] (since f is continuously differentiable), hence f' in R[0,2].

cards.label: Mark yourself 2 of 3 · up to 1 mark
cards.q: Did you apply the First Form of FTC to get integral of f' from 0 to 2 equal to 5?

options.t: Integral of f' equals f(2) - f(0) = 4 - (-1) = 5
FTC used but the values f(2) and f(0) are substituted wrongly
No FTC step

cards.why: Full marks need integral f' = f(2) - f(0) = 4 - (-1) = 5.

cards.label: Mark yourself 3 of 3 · up to 1 mark
cards.q: Did you bound the integral above by 4 and state the contradiction 5 <= 4?

options.t: f' <= 2 gives integral f' <= 2 x 2 = 4; contradiction 5 <= 4
Upper bound 4 found but the contradiction is not stated
No upper bound

cards.why: Full marks need f' <= 2 giving integral f' <= 2 x 2 = 4, and the contradiction 5 <= 4.

cards.label: Model answer 1 of 3
cards.title: Assume f exists
cards.body: Suppose such a function \(f\) exists. Since \(f\) is continuously differentiable, \(f'\) is continuous on \([0,2]\), so \(f' \in \mathcal{R}[0,2]\).

cards.label: Model answer 2 of 3
cards.title: First Form of FTC
cards.body: By the First Form of the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus, \(\int_0^2 f' = f(2) - f(0) = 4 - (-1) = 5\).

cards.label: Model answer 3 of 3
cards.title: Contradiction
cards.body: The condition \(f'(x) \le 2\) and monotonicity give \(\int_0^2 f' \le 2 \times 2 = 4\). But \(5 \le 4\) is false, so no such function exists.

cards.label: Key line
cards.title: Key line
cards.body: 5 ≤ 4 is false, so no such f exists.

cards.label: Key points
cards.title: Remember
points: f' continuous implies f' in R[a,b].
First Form of FTC: integral of f' = f(b) - f(a).
f' <= 2 gives integral of f' <= 2(b-a) = 4.
5 <= 4 is false, so no such function exists.

cards.label: Model answer 1 of 5
cards.title: Statement
cards.body: Let \(f \in \mathcal{R}[a,b]\), and let \(F : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}\) be continuous on \([a,b]\) with \(F'(x) = f(x)\) for all \(x \in (a,b)\) except at the points of a finite set E. Then \(\int_a^b f = F(b) - F(a)\).

cards.label: Model answer 2 of 5
cards.title: Set-up
cards.body: Let \(L = \int_a^b f\) and \(\varepsilon > 0\). Since f is integrable, there is \(\eta > 0\) with \(|S(f;P) - L| < \varepsilon\) for every tagged partition P with \(\|P\| < \eta\). Fix such a partition and refine it so that it contains all points of E. Refining does not increase the norm.

cards.label: Model answer 3 of 5
cards.title: Mean Value Theorem
cards.body: On each subinterval \([x_{i-1}, x_i]\), F is continuous and differentiable in the interior, since E is among the partition points. By the Mean Value Theorem there is \(u_i \in (x_{i-1}, x_i)\) with \(F(x_i) - F(x_{i-1}) = f(u_i)(x_i - x_{i-1})\), because \(u_i\) is not in E and so \(F'(u_i) = f(u_i)\).

cards.label: Model answer 4 of 5
cards.title: Telescoping sum
cards.body: Summing over i, the left side telescopes: \(F(b) - F(a) = \sum_{i=1}^n f(u_i)(x_i - x_{i-1})\). This is a Riemann sum for f over a tagged partition of norm below \(\eta\), so \(|F(b) - F(a) - L| < \varepsilon\).

cards.label: Model answer 1 of 7
cards.title: Cauchy Criterion
cards.body: A function \(f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}\) is Riemann integrable on \([a,b]\) if and only if for every \(\varepsilon > 0\) there is \(\eta > 0\) such that \(|S(f;P) - S(f;Q)| < \varepsilon\) for all tagged partitions P and Q of \([a,b]\) with \(\|P\| < \eta\) and \(\|Q\| < \eta\).

cards.label: Model answer 2 of 7
cards.title: Only if
cards.body: Suppose \(f \in \mathcal{R}[a,b]\) with integral L. Given \(\varepsilon > 0\), take \(\eta\) with \(|S(f;P) - L| < \varepsilon/2\) whenever \(\|P\| < \eta\). For such P and Q, \(|S(f;P) - S(f;Q)| \le |S(f;P) - L| + |L - S(f;Q)| < \varepsilon\).

cards.label: Model answer 3 of 7
cards.title: If: construction
cards.body: Assume the criterion holds, and choose \(\eta_{1/k}\) for each k. For each n choose a tagged partition \(P_n\) with \(\|P_n\| < \min\{\eta_{1/k} : k \le n\}\) and \(\|P_n\| < 1/n\). For \(m, n \ge N\), both norms are below \(\eta_{1/N}\), so \(|S(f;P_m) - S(f;P_n)| < 1/N\). Hence \(S(f;P_n)\) is Cauchy and converges to some A.

cards.label: Model answer 4 of 7
cards.title: If: conclusion
cards.body: Let \(\varepsilon > 0\) and choose N with \(1/N < \min\{\varepsilon/2, \eta_{\varepsilon/2}\}\). Then \(\|P_N\| < \eta_{\varepsilon/2}\), and \(|S(f;P_N) - A| \le 1/N < \varepsilon/2\). For \(\|P\| < \eta_{\varepsilon/2}\), \(|S(f;P) - A| < \varepsilon\). So f is integrable with integral A.

cards.title: Dirichlet conclusion
cards.body: Then \(S(f;P) = 1\) and \(S(f;Q) = 0\), so \(|S(f;P) - S(f;Q)| = 1 \ge \tfrac12 = \varepsilon_0\) for every \(\eta > 0\). The Cauchy Criterion fails, so f is not Riemann integrable on \([0,1]\).

cards.label: Model answer 7 of 7
cards.title: Remark
cards.body: The upper integral of f is 1 and the lower integral is 0. These differ, so no common value exists, which is another way to see that f is not integrable.

cards.title: Question 20
cards.q:
(a) Let \(f : [a, b] \to \mathbb{R}\) and let \(c \in (a, b)\). Prove that \(f \in \mathcal{R}[a, b]\) if and only if its restrictions to \([a, c]\) and \([c, b]\) are both Riemann integrable, and in this case \(\int_a^b f = \int_a^c f + \int_c^b f\).
(b) If \(f \in \mathcal{R}[a, b]\) and \([c, d] \subseteq [a, b]\), prove that the restriction of \(f\) to \([c, d]\) is in \(\mathcal{R}[c, d]\).

cards.label: Model answer 2 of 8
cards.title: Only if: set-up
cards.body: Suppose \(f \in \mathcal{R}[a,b]\) and \(\varepsilon > 0\). Take \(\eta\) from the Cauchy Criterion on \([a,b]\). Take tagged partitions \(P_1, Q_1\) of \([a,c]\) with norm below \(\eta\), and fix a tagged partition \(P_2\) of \([c,b]\) with norm below \(\eta\).

cards.label: Model answer 3 of 8
cards.title: Only if: conclusion
cards.body: The partitions \(P_1 \cup P_2\) and \(Q_1 \cup P_2\) of \([a,b]\) have norm below \(\eta\). The common sum \(S(f;P_2)\) cancels, so \(|S(f;P_1) - S(f;Q_1)| = |S(f;P_1 \cup P_2) - S(f;Q_1 \cup P_2)| < \varepsilon\). The Cauchy Criterion holds on \([a,c]\), and the same argument works on \([c,b]\).

cards.label: Model answer 4 of 8
cards.title: If: set-up
cards.body: Let \(f_1 = f|_{[a,c]}\) and \(f_2 = f|_{[c,b]}\) be integrable with integrals \(L_1\) and \(L_2\). Integrable functions are bounded, so \(|f(x)| \le M\) on \([a,b]\) for some \(M > 0\). Given \(\varepsilon > 0\), let \(\eta'\) work for \(\varepsilon/3\) on both pieces, and put \(\eta = \min\{\eta', \varepsilon/(6M)\}\).

cards.label: Model answer 5 of 8
cards.title: If: c a partition point
cards.body: Let P be a tagged partition of \([a,b]\) with \(\|P\| < \eta\) having c as one of its points. Then \(P = P_1 \cup P_2\), where \(P_1\) and \(P_2\) are tagged partitions of \([a,c]\) and \([c,b]\). So \(S(f;P) = S(f_1;P_1) + S(f_2;P_2)\), and \(|S(f;P) - (L_1 + L_2)| < \varepsilon/3 + \varepsilon/3 = 2\varepsilon/3\).

cards.label: Model answer 6 of 8
cards.title: If: c inside a subinterval
cards.body: Suppose c lies inside \([x_{k-1}, x_k]\), with tag \(t_k\). Add c to P, giving the piece containing \(t_k\) the tag \(t_k\) and the other piece the tag c. Only the k-th term changes, by at most \(2M\|P\| < \varepsilon/3\). The refined sum is within \(2\varepsilon/3\) of \(L_1 + L_2\), so \(|S(f;P) - (L_1 + L_2)| < \varepsilon\).

cards.label: Model answer 7 of 8
cards.title: Formula
cards.body: So for each \(\varepsilon > 0\) there is \(\eta > 0\) with \(|S(f;P) - (L_1 + L_2)| < \varepsilon\) for all tagged partitions P of \([a,b]\) with norm below \(\eta\). Hence \(f \in \mathcal{R}[a,b]\) and \(\int_a^b f = \int_a^c f + \int_c^b f\).

cards.label: Model answer 8 of 8
cards.title: Part (b)
cards.body: Let \([c,d] \subseteq [a,b]\). If \(d < b\), the only if part of (a) at d gives \(f|_{[a,d]} \in \mathcal{R}[a,d]\). If \(c > a\), the only if part at c, applied to that restriction, gives \(f|_{[c,d]} \in \mathcal{R}[c,d]\). If \(c = a\) and \(d = b\), there is nothing to prove.

cards.label: Key points
cards.title: Remember
points: Additivity: f is in R[a,b] iff both restrictions to [a,c] and [c,b] are integrable.
Only if: fix one partition of [c,b]; the common sum cancels in the difference.
If: splitting at c gives eps/3 + eps/3; c inside a subinterval costs under eps/3.
Choose eta = min(eta', eps/(6M)), so that 2M times the norm is below eps/3.
Restrictions of an integrable function to subintervals are integrable.
